questiontext.text: Which action best begins integrated portfolio preparation?

answer.text: List required parts and mark each present, missing, or needing revision.

questiontext.text: Which piece belongs in a final portfolio?

answer.text: A revised piece that shows a specific craft skill and reader effect.
A piece with no title and no revision.
A favorite piece the writer cannot explain.

questiontext.text: A portfolio statement discusses voice. Which evidence best matches it?

answer.text: A random image pasted beside the title.
A revised story excerpt where dialogue and sentence rhythm reveal character voice.
A file name with no writing attached.
A paragraph saying the writer worked hard.

questiontext.text: Which portfolio order has the clearest purpose?

answer.text: Alphabetical by file name with no explanation.
Longest to shortest only because length matters most.
Story first for revised dialogue, poem second for voice through rhythm, statement last to explain growth.

questiontext.text: Which note is most useful during a readiness pass?

answer.text: Preview script and make character labels consistent.

questiontext.text: How should an author statement connect to selected pieces?

answer.text: It should name skills the reader can see in the portfolio.

questiontext.text: Which presentation choice best supports the portfolio?

answer.text: Read the longest excerpt regardless of purpose.
Choose one excerpt that shows a craft choice connected to portfolio growth.

questiontext.text: Which problem should be fixed before final publication?

answer.text: The writer can explain the piece clearly.
The final file includes bracketed notes that say add ending later.

questiontext.text: What makes a portfolio integrated?

answer.text: The selected pieces, statement, revision evidence, and presentation plan connect to shared growth.

questiontext.text: Which answer best explains reader effect?

answer.text: I put this first because I found it first.
I revised the line breaks so the reader pauses before the speaker's decision.

questiontext.text: A student marks "needs revision" beside the presentation plan. What should come next?

answer.text: Write the exact missing action, such as add listening focus.

questiontext.text: Which choice shows revision evidence?

answer.text: A draft and final version with a note explaining how feedback improved dialogue.
A final piece with no explanation and no draft trail.

questiontext.text: Which author rationale is strongest?

answer.text: I included this because it was easy.
I included this because it is first alphabetically.
I included this because I needed another page.
I included this poem because revising the image pattern made the speaker's change clearer.

questiontext.text: Which statement describes publication formatting?

answer.text: Preparing the piece with title, spacing, labels, conventions, and file readiness.

questiontext.text: What should a student do if the portfolio order feels random?

answer.text: Create a reader-focused order and explain the reason.

questiontext.text: Which checkpoint response shows mastery?

answer.text: My portfolio order moves from revised story to poem to statement so readers see voice growth across genres.
I am done because I clicked submit.

questiontext.text: Which final presentation note is strongest?

answer.text: I do not know what to listen for.
Listen for how the clipped dialogue creates tension after the narrator avoids the question.

questiontext.text: Which issue is a portfolio completeness problem?
Why should the student avoid vague notes like "fix portfolio"?

answer.text: They do not identify the exact action needed.

questiontext.text: Which answer best connects publication and presentation?

answer.text: The portfolio shows the final work, and the presentation explains how selected craft choices work.
Publication means no one reads the piece.

questiontext.text: Which choice should be removed from a final portfolio file?
Which answer is strongest when explaining a selected excerpt?

answer.text: I selected it because it is confusing.
I selected it because it shows the exact revision I describe in my statement.
I selected it but will not explain it.

questiontext.text: Which readiness pass checks genre-specific format?

answer.text: Check poems for intentional line breaks and scripts for clear character labels.

questiontext.text: A student says the statement and portfolio do not match. What is the best fix?

answer.text: Align the statement's claims with evidence in the selected pieces.

questiontext.text: Which final decision best shows Unit 6 integration?

answer.text: Submit publication-ready pieces, a connected author statement, revision evidence, and a presentation plan with craft focus.

questiontext.text: Portfolio context: A writer says, "I chose this poem because I like it." What is the best revision of the selection reason?

answer.text: I chose this poem because it was short.
I chose this poem because I found it first.
I chose this poem because the revised final image shows stronger control of imagery and emotion.
I chose no pieces because portfolios do not need writing.

questiontext.text: Which item is the strongest evidence for a craft rationale?

answer.text: A before-and-after revision that changes "I was lonely" into a specific bus stop image.
A sentence saying the piece is good.

questiontext.text: Which three parts belong in a complete craft rationale?

answer.text: Favorite line, favorite color, and page number.

questiontext.text: Author statement: "I guess this poem is fine, and people can think whatever." What is the main tone problem?
Which author statement sentence has the strongest tone?

answer.text: This is good and nobody should question it.
I revised this piece to make the speaker's uncertainty clearer through repeated images.

questiontext.text: Story problem: Readers do not understand why Ellis leaves at the end. Which revision best fits?

answer.text: Add one action showing Ellis choosing to leave before the final line.

questiontext.text: Story problem: A suspense scene moves too quickly. Which revision best improves pacing?

answer.text: Add action beats as the character listens at the door and watches the light shift.

questiontext.text: Poem problem: The line says, "I felt sad." Feedback asks for a stronger image. Which revision best fits?

answer.text: Rain gathered on the sill until the glass forgot the street.

questiontext.text: Poem problem: The final choice happens too quickly. Which revision best uses line breaks?

answer.text: Place the final phrase on its own line so the reader pauses before the decision.
Change the poem into a grocery list.

questiontext.text: A student is preparing a poem for digital publication. Which formatting choice best supports the genre?

answer.text: Put the entire poem in one paragraph so it uses less space.
Remove the title because poems do not need one.
Keep the title clear and preserve purposeful line and stanza breaks.

questiontext.text: A short story draft appears as one long block of text with dialogue inside the same paragraph. What should the writer do first?

answer.text: Add paragraph breaks when the speaker changes and when the action shifts.
Change every sentence to a different font.
Add extra blank lines after every sentence.

questiontext.text: An author presentation begins with a short story excerpt. Which opening best prepares the audience?

answer.text: I am reading something I wrote, and that is all you need to know.
My piece is a short story called The Last Bus. Listen for the short sentences because they show panic.
This is long, so I will explain every event before reading.
I picked this because it is my favorite.

questiontext.text: Which excerpt choice is strongest for an author presentation?

answer.text: The longest section, even if it needs ten minutes of explanation.
A random middle section with no context.
A short section that clearly shows a craft choice and can be understood with brief context.
The first page only because first pages are always best.

questiontext.text: Which portfolio choice is strongest?

answer.text: Choose the longest piece only because it fills space.
Choose the favorite piece with no explanation.
Choose a piece with unresolved draft comments.
Choose a revised piece that shows clear craft growth and can be explained.

questiontext.text: A student notices the author statement discusses imagery, but no selected piece shows imagery. What should the student do?

answer.text: Revise the statement or portfolio so the evidence and explanation match.
Leave the mismatch because readers will guess.
Remove all craft language from the statement.
